articles.title: Volunteer scheme credited with changing man's life
articles.summary: Michael Reynolds, 27, says the scheme helps him to "get away from day-to-day life".
articles.content:
A programme designed to get people with additional needs back into work, has been credited with transforming a 27-year-old man's life.

Michael Reynolds, from Shawbury, used to work in catering before he was made redundant during the coronavirus pandemic.

Nine months ago, he started volunteering at Fordhall Farm in Market Drayton, which his family said brought him out of a difficult place.

Reynolds added it helped him to "get away from day-to-day life," and acted as "a day out".

He is one of more than 1,350 young people who have been supported through an employability and enterprise programme, delivered by four charities across Shropshire.

After being referred by his Jobcentre work coach, Reynolds joined up at a time where he was struggling with his mental health, confidence and a sense of direction.

He originally went with his mother but he eventually gained the confidence to go by himself.

Since then, he said he learned a lot being a part of the group.

"I have done all sorts, all sorts, trimming back brambles, conservation work, tidying up, setting up for events."

He added that since joining, he developed a passion for the environment and wanted to continue working in conservation in the future.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a volunteer scheme that has positively impacted a young man's mental health, confidence, and employability by engaging him in meaningful conservation work. The program supports over 1,350 young people, indicating a broad social benefit. It focuses on a clear, inspiring story of personal transformation through community support and environmental engagement.

articles.title: 'South Asian programmes helped us settle into our new lives'
articles.summary: Early South Asian programming included music and practical tips to settle into British life.
articles.content:
Those same programmes meant just as much to Krishna Devi, who arrived in 1967 and lived in Harehills, another inner-city neighbourhood in Leeds.

Krishna was also just 17 when she came from India, joining her husband and his family.

"It wasn't easy," Krishna says. "We didn't understand English and they didn't understand Punjabi."

One programme helped new arrivals learn the basics: 'Look, Listen and Speak', a BBC English learning series widely used at that time.

"They used to teach us word by word. They taught us how to cross the road. Look left, right."

Even simple tasks could feel unfamiliar.

"When I went to the shops, I didn't know how much things cost. I'd put the money out on my hand and let the shopkeeper take however much it was."

Like Nirmala, the programme she looked forward to most was Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan.

"There was one Hindi song in that half hour. We waited for it."

Asked why those songs mattered so much, her answer is simple.

"Because it was our language. That half hour made us forget everything else."

Her Sundays followed a familiar pattern: chai, parathas and three generations gathered around a television.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the positive impact of early South Asian programming in helping immigrants settle into British life by providing language learning and cultural connection, which has meaningful social and emotional benefits for a broad immigrant community.
articles.personality_title: Early South Asian TV helped new immigrants settle in Britain
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the 1960s and 1970s, many South Asian families moved to Britain. They faced challenges like language barriers and unfamiliar customs as they tried to build new lives.

**What happened** – South Asian TV programmes in Britain offered help by teaching English and sharing cultural content. For example, a BBC show called 'Look, Listen and Speak' taught basic English and everyday skills, like how to cross the street safely. Another popular show, 'Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan', included Hindi songs that reminded viewers of home.

**Impact** – These programmes made a big difference for people like Krishna Devi, who arrived in Britain at 17. They helped her and others understand English better and feel connected to their culture. The shows also eased everyday tasks that felt confusing at first, such as shopping or crossing roads. Watching familiar songs and language on TV created comfort and a sense of belonging.

**What's next step** – These early programmes set an example for future media to support immigrants by combining practical help with cultural connection. Similar efforts today can continue to assist new arrivals in adjusting to life in a new country.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Early South Asian TV shows combined language lessons and cultural traditions to help immigrants feel at home in Britain.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les premières émissions sud-asiatiques ont aidé les nouveaux immigrants à s'installer en Grande-Bretagne
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dans les années 1960 et 1970, de nombreuses familles sud-asiatiques ont émigré en Grande-Bretagne. Elles ont rencontré des difficultés comme la barrière de la langue et des coutumes inconnues en essayant de construire une nouvelle vie.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Les émissions télévisées sud-asiatiques en Grande-Bretagne ont offert de l'aide en enseignant l'anglais et en partageant du contenu culturel. Par exemple, une émission de la BBC appelée « Look, Listen and Speak » enseignait l'anglais de base et des compétences quotidiennes, comme traverser la rue en toute sécurité. Une autre émission populaire, « Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan », comprenait des chansons en hindi qui rappelaient aux téléspectateurs leur pays d'origine.

**Impact** – Ces programmes ont eu un grand impact pour des personnes comme Krishna Devi, arrivée en Grande-Bretagne à 17 ans. Ils les ont aidés à mieux comprendre l'anglais et à rester connectés à leur culture. Les émissions ont aussi facilité des tâches quotidiennes qui semblaient compliquées au début, comme faire les courses ou traverser la rue. Regarder des chansons et une langue familières à la télévision créait du réconfort et un sentiment d'appartenance.

**Prochaine étape** – Ces premières émissions ont montré l'exemple pour les médias futurs afin de soutenir les immigrants en combinant aide pratique et lien culturel. Des efforts similaires aujourd'hui peuvent continuer à aider les nouveaux arrivants à s'adapter à la vie dans un nouveau pays.

**Une phrase clé** – Les premières émissions télévisées sud-asiatiques ont mêlé cours de langue et traditions culturelles pour aider les immigrants à se sentir chez eux en Grande-Bretagne.
articles.personality_title_es: Los primeros programas sudasiáticos ayudaron a los nuevos inmigrantes a adaptarse en Gran Bretaña
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En las décadas de 1960 y 1970, muchas familias sudasiáticas se mudaron a Gran Bretaña. Enfrentaron desafíos como la barrera del idioma y costumbres desconocidas mientras intentaban construir una nueva vida.

**Qué pasó** – Los programas de televisión sudasiáticos en Gran Bretaña ofrecieron ayuda enseñando inglés y compartiendo contenido cultural. Por ejemplo, un programa de la BBC llamado 'Look, Listen and Speak' enseñaba inglés básico y habilidades cotidianas, como cruzar la calle con seguridad. Otro programa popular, 'Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan', incluía canciones en hindi que recordaban a los espectadores su hogar.

**Impacto** – Estos programas marcaron una gran diferencia para personas como Krishna Devi, que llegó a Gran Bretaña con 17 años. Les ayudaron a entender mejor el inglés y a mantenerse conectados con su cultura. Los programas también facilitaron tareas diarias que al principio parecían confusas, como hacer compras o cruzar la calle. Ver canciones y el idioma familiar en la televisión creó comodidad y un sentido de pertenencia.

**Próximo paso** – Estos primeros programas sentaron un ejemplo para que los medios futuros apoyen a los inmigrantes combinando ayuda práctica con conexión cultural. Esfuerzos similares hoy pueden seguir ayudando a los recién llegados a adaptarse a la vida en un nuevo país.

**Una frase clave** – Los primeros programas de televisión sudasiáticos combinaron lecciones de idioma y tradiciones culturales para ayudar a los inmigrantes a sentirse en casa en Gran Bretaña.
